analysis.one_liner: Bans rental car companies from charging renters for vehicle damage or selling collision damage waivers.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have stopped rental companies from holding short-term renters liable for car damage, never got a hearing or vote and died in a House subcommittee after referral.
analysis.plain_summary: Rental car companies commonly held renters responsible for damage to the rented car and then sold them a costly extra 'collision damage waiver' to escape that liability. This bill would have banned both practices for rentals of 30 days or less: companies could only charge for damage in a narrow set of cases like drunk driving, street racing, or fraud; they could not sell waivers at all; they could not sue a renter outside the renter's home state; and they could not demand a security deposit. Violations would carry a $500 to $1,000 penalty each.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone renting a car for 30 days or less. They would no longer face unlimited liability for damage they did not cause through serious misconduct, would not be pressured at the counter to buy a waiver, and could not be sued far from home or held hostage by a security deposit.

how_it_helps.text: Rental companies could not hold an authorized driver liable for damage to the rented vehicle except in narrow cases such as intoxication, speed contests, fraud, criminal use, or unauthorized use outside the U.S. and Canada [S3].
The companies would be prohibited from selling collision damage waivers for the remaining exceptions or for any deductible, ending the counter sale of this add-on [S2] [S3].
Companies could only sue a U.S.-resident renter for damage in the renter's home state, and could not require or request any security deposit for damage [S2] [S3].
Each violation would carry a penalty of $500 to $1,000, enforceable by courts or state agencies [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Rental car companies, which would lose waiver sales revenue and would bear ordinary collision costs themselves, likely passing some of that into daily rental rates. Renters who have no other coverage and relied on buying the waiver would lose that option.

drawbacks.text: Renters with no personal auto insurance or credit-card collision coverage would lose the ability to buy damage protection at the counter, leaving them with no way to insure the rented vehicle under this bill's terms [S3].
Rental companies would absorb the cost of ordinary damage on their fleets and could be expected to raise daily rates to cover it, spreading the cost to all renters including careful ones [S3].
The penalties are modest ($500-$1,000 per violation), which could limit how strongly companies felt compelled to comply [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a real consumer annoyance: being billed for damage and pressured into an expensive add-on at the rental counter. Its complete ban on selling waivers is the weak point, because renters without other coverage would have no way to buy protection. Weighing that, it was a consumer-friendly but somewhat blunt instrument that never advanced far enough to be refined.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then passed down to a consumer protection subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, no vote, and no further action until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Lynn Martin of Illinois introduced the Collision Damage Waiver Act on February 9, 1989, joined by Rep. Dennis Eckart [S1] [S3] [S5].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S5].
On February 27, 1989, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Consumer Protection and Competitiveness [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S5].
The bill attracted 21 cosponsors, 17 House Democrats and 4 House Republicans [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Rental car companies came out ahead: because the bill never advanced, they kept the right to hold renters liable for damage and to sell collision damage waivers at the counter. Renters continued to face those charges.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start: a Republican sponsor introduced it with a Democratic co-introducer, and the 21 cosponsors split 17 Democrats and 4 Republicans. There is no record of floor opposition because the bill never reached a vote.

industries.note: The bill would end their ability to charge renters for vehicle damage and would ban the sale of collision damage waivers, a profitable counter add-on. Their gain under the current system comes directly from charges ordinary renters bear.
